name: Dian Cécht
text: Dian Cécht stands as the principal healing god of the ancient Irish. The form Diancécht is also used. His name may mean rolling quickly forward or swift power. He served the Tuatha Dé Danann as their sage of leechcraft. The old word leechcraft meant the practice of medicine. Dian Cécht was father of Étan and father of Cian. He was therefore grandfather of Lug Lámfhota. In the Cath Maige Tuired his healing spring restored every wounded man save those who had been beheaded. He also forged a silver limb with working digits for the wounded Nuadu. Nuadu was afterwards called Nuadu Airgedlámh. The epithet Airgedlámh means of the silver hand or arm. The silver limb did not suffice to restore Nuadu to kingship. Dian Cécht's son Miach later fashioned Nuadu an arm of flesh. The flesh-arm at last let Nuadu ascend to power. Dian Cécht then killed Miach out of jealousy at his greater skill. He also broke up his daughter Airmid's ordering of magical herbs. Mac Cécht appears to be a euhemerized form of Dian Cécht. The porridge of Dian Cécht appears in modern folklore as a cure. The cure takes hazel nuts, dandelion, woodsorrel, chickweed, and oatmeal. The charms of Dian Cécht were still invoked in Christian Ireland into the eighth century.

okr.objective: Dian Cécht as the physician of the Tuatha Dé Danann, healer of Nuadu, and jealous father of Miach.
key_results: Dian Cécht was the chief healing god of the Tuatha Dé Danann.
His healing spring could restore every wounded man except the beheaded.
He made the silver arm for Nuadu, who became Nuadu Airgedlámh.
His son Miach later made Nuadu a flesh arm and Dian Cécht killed him in jealousy.
He disrupted his daughter Airmid's ordering of the healing herbs.
Mac Cécht appears to be a euhemerized form of Dian Cécht.
His charms survived in Christian use into the eighth century.
